title: An alternative path for artificial intelligence in Africa
abstract: African governments face a perceived choice between investing in costly national data centers and dependence on foreign technology providers. Both options rest on assumptions that the evidence no longer supports. We argue for a third path, distributed sovereignty: cooperative infrastructure designed for African conditions.

title: From broken circuits to growing graphite: A new role for electromigration
abstract: Inside electronic devices, electric current can gradually displace atoms within tiny metal connections, creating gaps or unwanted accumulations that eventually cause circuits to fail. This phenomenon, known as electromigration, has long been regarded as a reliability problem that engineers must work to prevent. Yet the ability of an electric current to move atoms also raises the possibility of putting that movement to constructive use, directing atoms through a material rather than allowing them to migrate uncontrollably.

title: Comment on “Hybrid Graph–Machine Learning Framework for Accurate and Interpretable Band Gap Prediction”
abstract: Aydin et al. reported R2 = 0.921 for band gap prediction using hybrid graph neural networks. Reproduction shows this performance is inflated by data leakage from post-DFT proxies (is_metal, is_gap_direct) and embedding contamination. Controlled ablations reveal a genuine GNN gain of 0.08–0.11 in R2, while leakage contributes ∼0.06, lowering honest performance to 0.82–0.86 R2 (MAE 0.28–0.30 eV).
venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling

title: Defect-Mediated On–Off Growth in Tautomeric Crystallization: The Curious Case of Theophylline Monohydrate
abstract: Crystal growth is inherently sensitive to interfacial structure, yet it remains poorly understood how intrinsic molecular heterogeneity in tautomeric materials translates into dynamic growth behaviors. Here, we combine microfluidics, in situ atomic force microscopy (AFM), molecular dynamics (MD), and density functional theory (DFT) to investigate the crystallization of theophylline monohydrate, which exhibits a minor tautomer (TP-N9, percent-level) coexisting in growth solutions with the dominant lattice-forming species (TP-N7).
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: RxnNet: An AI Framework for Reaction Mechanism Discovery─A Case Study in Mass Spectrometry
abstract: Understanding complex multistep reaction mechanisms remains a major challenge, particularly in the interpretation of tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) data, where fragmentation pathways often involve rearrangements and competing reaction channels. Here, we extend the application of RxnNet, a mechanistically driven framework for automated reaction discovery, to gas-phase fragmentation processes.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: Rare-Earth Oxysulfides RE2O2S as Model Mixed-Anion-Frustrated Magnets
abstract: The study of low-dimensional and anisotropic magnetism is a promising avenue for the discovery of novel quantum phenomena. Mixed-anion materials, defined by the coordination of metal cations by two or more distinct anionic species, provide an intrinsically anisotropic platform for the tuning of structural, magnetic, and electronic properties. In this work, we report the synthesis and characterization of a family of rare-earth oxysulfide (RE2O2S) antiferromagnets (AFM) possessing a triangular-bilayer slab lattice geometry.

title: Shake It Off: Abl Kinase Regulatory Domain Dynamics Explain Conformational Changes upon Activation
abstract: Abl kinase is a major molecular target for chronic myeloid leukemia therapy. Its activity is tightly controlled by its regulatory module, composed of the SH3 and SH2 domains and the SH2–kinase linker. Although the assembled autoinhibited and extended active conformations have been structurally characterized, the molecular pathway connecting these states remains poorly understood. Simulations initiated from the end point structures failed to sample the complete transition, even when Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) was employed to enhance conformational sampling. To overcome this limitation, we combined multiscale modeling with extensive molecular dynamics simulations and Markov state modeling to reconstruct the Abl disassembly pathway. The resulting kinetic landscape revealed two coupled conformational equilibria: a faster exchange between the canonical assembled state and an intermediate ensemble that captures the initial rotation of the regulatory module, and a slower transition toward the extended state, characterized by migration of the regulatory module atop the kinase domain N-lobe. The assembled ensemble is favored (∼88% of the equilibrium population), with the canonical autoinhibited arrangement alone accounting for approximately 60%, while early disassembly disrupts the E98–K294 and SH3–linker interactions and releases Y226 from its protective interactions, while Y70 remains accessible through the intrinsic dynamics of the SH3 domain. By revealing how these phosphorylation-sensitive residues become accessible during the earliest stages of disassembly, our model provides a mechanistic framework for Abl activation and identifies regulatory interfaces as potential targets for allosteric stabilization of the autoinhibited state.
venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling

title: Atomically Confined Structural Self-Compensation at Grain Boundaries in Ba-Based Layered Proton Conductors
abstract: Ion transport and interfacial stability in oxide materials are strongly influenced by the electrostatics that develop at grain boundaries. In conventional ABO3-type perovskites, grain boundary resistance is well-explained by space-charge effects, in which a positively charged grain boundary core is compensated by the accumulation of negatively charged acceptor dopants. By contrast, the compensation mechanism in recently developed Ba-based layered perovskites has remained unclear. In this study, by directly resolving the grain boundary atomic structure of this material class, we identify a previously unrecognized, structurally confined charge-compensation mode. Using atomic-resolution imaging, spatially resolved electron energy-loss spectroscopy, density functional theory, Poisson–Cahn calculations, and impedance spectroscopy, we show that acceptor-doped BaZrO3 compensates its grain boundary through diffuse dopant segregation, whereas layered Ba2LuAlO5 and Ba5Er2Al2ZrO13, which possess intrinsically oxygen-deficient frameworks, instead form a BaLnO3-δ-type layer (Ln = lanthanide) immediately adjacent to the grain boundary core. Relative to the diffuse space-charge layer in BZY82, this atomically localized compensation confines the compensating charge to a single structural block, thereby lowering the electrostatic barrier and the grain boundary activation energy for proton transport. These findings establish spatially confined structural compensation as a key determinant of grain boundary charge balance in layered perovskites and provide a general design principle for engineering next-generation, high-performance Ba-based protonic electrolytes.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: A Unified Asymmetric Approach to Tetracyclic Diterpenoids via Ring Reconstruction Strategy
abstract: Tetracyclic diterpenoids exhibit intricate densely fused and bridged polycyclic architectures and diverse biological profiles, yet their collective asymmetric synthesis from a unified precursor remains a formidable challenge due to immense topological barriers between distinct scaffolds. Herein, we report a divergent asymmetric synthesis of the tetracyclic diterpenoid family driven by a “ring reconstruction” strategy.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Awakening Latent Diradicals to Enhance Antiferromagnetic Coupling between Localized Organic Spin Centers
abstract: Connecting persistent radicals through π-conjugated linkers provides a promising route for developing organic magnetic systems. However, the simultaneous realization of localized addressable spins and thermally robust antiferromagnetic (AFM) coupling remains challenging. Conventional approaches based on quinoidal versus aromatic resonance forms impose electronic constraints that limit access to this regime. Here, we introduce a molecular design principle in which the latent open-shell character of selected heterocyclic linkers is activated to significantly strengthen AFM interactions between localized radical centers. First-principles calculations reveal that this enhancement: i) originates from increased linker spin polarization acting synergistically with partial quinoidalization, and ii) is robust across a series of diradicals combining an expandable family of linkers with representative persistent radicals. We identify diradicals displaying pronounced open-shell character with unusually large singlet–triplet energy gaps typically associated with closed-shell systems. Extending this concept to two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks, we further show that our approach translates from discrete molecules to strongly AFM materials.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Thermally driven multiple sliding states and avalanche dynamics in rhombohedral Pb(TaSe2)2 nanoflakes
abstract: Interlayer sliding in van der Waals materials offers a promising route to control functional properties, yet a comprehensive understanding of the complex collective domain dynamics governing these transitions remains challenging. Here, we investigate thermally driven sliding dynamics in Pb(TaSe2)2 nanoflakes, incorporating transport and atomic-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) measurements. Reducing the flake thickness induces multiple stepwise resistance jumps with enhanced hysteresis, corresponding to transitions between stacking domains accompanied by ripplocations. Statistical analysis of the jumps reveals collective avalanche behavior of domain dynamics with universal power-law scaling, quantifying the domain motion. Harnessing these features, we demonstrate controllable, non-volatile multi-level resistive switching, including write/erase operations, via thermal cycling. These findings provide valuable insights into the sliding dynamics for various 2D materials, with significant implications for the development of slidetronics devices.

title: XevaDB enables AI-driven longitudinal pharmacogenomic modeling in patient-derived xenografts
abstract: Patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) are critical models for translational oncology, but their computational use is limited by fragmented pharmacogenomic data, inconsistent response annotations, and poor access to raw longitudinal tumour-volume measurements. Here we present XevaDB (xevadb.ca), a standardized platform designed to support machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) applications through the integration of longitudinal treatment and control-arm tumour growth curves with harmonized drug and gene annotations, response metrics, replicate-level experimental design, clinical…

title: Decoding C–O versus C–C Bond Selectivity in Nickel–Metallaphotoredox Carboxylic Acid Cross-Couplings
abstract: Understanding how catalytic systems dictate product selectivity is crucial for advancing cross-coupling chemistry. While nickel–photoredox dual catalysis has enabled both C─C and C─O bond formation from carboxylic acids and aryl halides under deceptively similar conditions, the mechanistic origins of this divergence have remained elusive. Here, we combine systematic experimentation with density functional theory (DFT) calculations and electrochemical analysis to uncover the key parameters that govern whether C─C or C─O bonds are formed. We show that the halide identity of the aryl electrophile exerts an influence: iodides strongly favor esterification via a low-barrier reductive elimination pathway, bromides promote decarboxylative C─C coupling, and chlorides, with higher C─O reductive elimination barriers, yield exclusively C─C products. Complementary experiments reveal that both photocatalyst loading and halide additives modulate selectivity, consistent with the computed energy landscapes. Together, these insights explain the divergent reactivity observed under seemingly similar conditions. By demonstrating how subtle changes in halide, photocatalyst, and additives toggle reaction outcomes, our study provides predictive design principles for exploiting carboxylic acids in nickel–photoredox catalysis.

title: Weakly coordinating anions and solvents break the conductivity-transference-solvation tradeoff
abstract: Lithium-metal batteries promise high energy density, but common electrolytes trade ionic conductivity against the share of current carried by lithium ions and against how strongly solvent binds those ions. We show that simultaneously weakening both interactions of the lithium ion, with solvent and with anion, relaxes this trade-off. Thus, a weakly coordinating perfluorinated alkoxyaluminate salt in liquefied fluoromethane conducts 39.2 mS cm$^{-1}$ at 25 $^\circ$C while maintaining a lithium-ion transference number of 0.71. Molecular dynamics simulations further reveal that the anion prevents persistent ion aggregation and lowers the salt's dissociation penalty. Consistent with these properties, nickel-rich cathode/lithium-metal anode full cells charge at 10C at room temperature and at 2C at $-40$ $^\circ$C. We advance coordination strength as a design axis for future energy storage devices.

title: Incorporating argumentation frameworks for LLM decision-making: Task-specific design and evaluation
abstract: Argumentation frameworks (AFs) provide explicit, formal mechanisms for representing and resolving conflicts and thus have been incorporated into large language model (LLM) decision-making. The benefits vary and depend on how arguments and their relations are constructed, evaluated, and incorporated into the decision process. {We abstract a workflow consisting of four stages based on existing argumentation-augmented methods} and investigate their design choices over tasks of debate-based decision-making and retrieval-based fact verification. Our evaluation with recent LLMs shows that existing methods do not consistently improve performance across the considered tasks. Motivated by this observation, we develop two task-specific methods. The first is called Qnt-Arg, which organizes arguments around the original speakers in debate materials and aggregates model-estimated argument strengths and candidate-answer priors under gradual semantics. The second is Qlt-Arg that uses credibility estimates to establish preferences between conflicting evidence items and applies grounded semantics to select acceptable evidence for subsequent LLM inference. We examine the roles of generative and decision models within the two methods. In the debate setting, Qnt-Arg consistently outperforms other argumentation-augmented methods across matched configurations; Qlt-Arg improves retrieval-based fact-verification performance compared with the baselines. These findings demonstrate the value of combining formal argumentation and LLM while highlighting the importance of aligning with tasks in argumentation construction, model selection, and the role of formal semantic reasoning.

title: Protein Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification
abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are commonly pretrained with likelihood-based objectives such as masked language modeling or denoising. These objectives capture sequence-level regularities, but can produce representations in which functional signals are entangled with non-functional variation (e.g., sequence identity, compositional bias, and frequent local motifs), creating a readout bottleneck for downstream function prediction. We introduce Functional Semantic Alignment via Representation Rectification (SAVR), a contrastive post-training method using Pfam family co-membership as a homology-guided discrete semantic signal to reshape PLM representations. SAVR reduces directional dominance and redistributes variance across embedding dimensions, decreasing variance concentration, and increasing effective dimensionality of the embedding covariance spectrum. Without observing any task-specific labels during post-training, SAVR achieves state-of-the-art results on Enzyme Commission (EC) benchmarks and competitive results on Gene Ontology (GO) benchmarks under frozen-backbone evaluation. These results suggest that homology-guided contrastive post-training can rectify PLM representation geometry and improve sequence-based protein function prediction.

title: Causal association and molecular mechanisms linking insomnia to late- onset Alzheimer’s disease: an integrated Mendelian randomization and transcriptomic analysis
abstract: Background Insomnia is consistently associated with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) in observational studies, but the causal relationship and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the causal relationship between insomnia and late-onset AD and to identify molecular pathways and candidate genes that may contribute to this association by integrating genetic causal inference with transcriptomics.

title: Palladium-Catalyzed Enantioselective Oxidative Remote (4 + 1)-Cyclization of 1,6-Enynes
abstract: Herein, we report a palladium-catalyzed enantioselective oxidative remote (4 + 1) cyclization of 1,6-enynes using PhI(OPiv)2 as the oxidant. Both Z- and E-enynes are competent substrates, affording the same cyclopentane-fused lactones and lactams with high efficiency, and excellent enantioselectivity is achieved using chiral pyridinyl oxazoline ligands. These cyclopentane-fused lactones can be readily transformed to other chiral cyclopentane derivatives. Notably, the use of TFE as the solvent is critical for attaining high chemoselectivity and enantioselectivity.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: De Novo Design of Enantioselective Artificial Metalloenzyme Photocatalysts
Mitragynine reduces symptoms of alcohol use disorder (and tinnitus) in a self-medication of rodents
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a major psychiatric disease. Available pharmacotherapies show rather modest compliance and efficacy. Tinnitus is a highly aversive hearing problem, that may arise from the same unsolved problems as AUD. Based on a patient report of Kratom, a Southeast Asian plant preparation, efficacy in the self-medication of AUD and tinnitus, we tested the main active Kratom alkaloid, mitragynine, for its therapeutic action in AUD mouse models covering various symptoms of the disease. We found that experimenter administered mitragynine (i.p.) inhibits well-established ongoing alcohol consumption in a social setting when alcohol is permanently available. Mitragynine also inhibits alcohol consumption in a non-social, isolated setting. While mitragynine did not work for prophylaxis during abstinence, it markedly attenuated the relapse to binge drinking with alcohol availability restricted to a limited time. Furthermore, mitragynine reduced alcohol seeking behaviour during its establishment as well as during retrieval from memory. It was also effective to attenuate its re-establishment after extinction. We found significant antidepressive effects of mitragynine, during alcohol withdrawal. To address the compliance problem for pharmacotherapies, we established a test that can monitor this and found that mice after a short training, learned to orally self-administer mitragynine hydrochloride leading to a strong reduction in voluntary alcohol drinking. In parallel, mitragynine reduced tinnitus after a noise trauma in a gerbil model. Together, these findings suggest that mitragynine may be used as a pharmacotherapy for AUD and tinnitus with an expected high compliance rate.

title: AdsNet: A Graph Neural Network for Direct Adsorption Energy Prediction
abstract: Fast and accurate prediction of adsorption energies is critical for high-throughput computational catalyst screening, existing methods compromise either on evaluation speed (full-graph machine learning potentials) or geometric sensitivity (coordination-based models like the alpha-scheme). Here, we present AdsNet, an equivariant graph neural network that directly predicts adsorption energies in a single forward pass, which operates on a local graph restricted only to adsorbate atoms and its immediate surface neighbors within a cutoff radius. This local graph formulation decouples computational complexity from total system size while encoding continuous geometric features (interatomic distances and directional vectors) enabling sensitivity to subtle variations in local bonding environments. AdsNet adopts a message-passing architecture with scalar and vector node features over multiple interaction layers. Trained on AdsTraj, a dataset of 33,920 density functional theory (DFT) calculated structures spanning 26 transition metals and 6 adsorbates (H*, C*, O*, CO*, OH*, HOCO*), the model achieves an adsorption energy root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 0.032 eV and a force RMSE of 0.047 eV/A. Analytic forces obtained via automatic differentiation enable structure relaxation through a projected gradient descent algorithm with adaptive line search, eliminating entire geometry optimizations. Additionally, AdsNet uniquely decomposes predicted adsorption energies into contributions from individual atoms within the local adsorbate graph - an interpretability feature unattainable with conventional machine-learning potentials. AdsNet thus establishes an accurate, highly efficient, and interpretable framework for large-scale adsorption energy prediction and local interface relaxation across various material surfaces.

title: MatVerse: A Foundation Model for Materials Science
abstract: Materials science involves highly heterogeneous scientific information, including textual knowledge, molecular and crystal structures, experimental characterization data, microscopy images, and structure-property relationships. Developing a general-purpose foundation model capable of understanding and reasoning over these diverse materials representations remains challenging. In this technical report, we introduce MatVerse, a materials foundation model built upon Intern-S2-Preview and further specialized through large-scale materials-domain post-training. We construct a large-scale multimodal training corpus covering materials knowledge, scientific reasoning, quantitative problem solving, structural understanding, and multimodal scientific interpretation. To improve domain adaptation, we develop a unified data construction pipeline combining teacher-guided reasoning distillation, scientific problem synthesis, consistency-based filtering, and retrieval-based multimodal data construction. We evaluate MatVerse on three representative materials-science benchmarks: our human-calibrated OmniMatBench, MatSciBench, and MaCBench. Results demonstrate consistent improvements after materials-specific post-training over the base model on all three benchmarks, alongside improved inference efficiency on calculation-intensive problems. These results show that targeted domain-specific post-training can effectively enhance scientific reasoning, materials knowledge understanding, and multimodal scientific capabilities of foundation models. MatVerse provides a unified language-and-vision interface for materials science and serves as a foundation for future AI-assisted materials research workflows.

title: GPU-Accelerated Secure Inference for Drug--Target Interaction Prediction
abstract: Deep learning models that predict drug--target interactions (DTI) can speed up drug discovery, but the candidate drugs they score are valuable intellectual property that their owners cannot reveal. Secure multiparty computation (MPC) lets two servers compute a prediction on a secret-shared drug, without either server learning the drug. However, secure inference of deep models is slow. Non-linear operations require communication between the servers, and MPC arithmetic does not map naturally to GPUs. In this paper, we present our solution to Track~III of the iDASH 2026 privacy and security competition, which asked for fast two-party secure DTI inference on GPUs. Our solution is built on the co-design of MPC-friendly models and MPC protocols. On the model side, we design SlimDTA, a DTI model that reduces the operations on the secret drug, and in particular the non-linear operations that require communication. On the protocol side, we build a GPU framework that evaluates the linear layers with additive secret sharing and the non-linear layers with function secret sharing, including a custom CUDA kernel for the comparisons. Our solution won first place in the competition, at under 10,ms per prediction on average, and its secure predictions match the plaintext model to within 0.02%.

title: PSTO: A PDE-structured transport operator with shared implicit updates for multiscale CDR systems
abstract: Multiscale convection-diffusion-reaction (CDR) systems couple spatial transport with local stiff reaction kinetics, making their numerical simulation computationally demanding. Conventional neural surrogates require costly coupled CDR training data, and their parameter counts scale with the number of transported variables, limiting scalability to high-dimensional CDR systems. Here we propose a PDE-Structured Transport Operator (PSTO) that learns convection--diffusion dynamics solely from reaction-free data. By embedding the PDE structure into the neural architecture, PSTO generalizes to full CDR systems at inference without retraining. A single transport operator block is shared across all transported variables and refined through relaxed fixed-point iterations, performing an implicit-like correction in latent space. This improves stability during recursive multi-step prediction without adding trainable parameters. We evaluate PSTO on three benchmarks: a canonical 2D CDR system, a multiscale Robertson counterflow flame, and a multiscale hydrogen planar jet flame. In every case, PSTO reduces the mean relative $L_2$ error after 100 coupled steps by at least 50% compared to the strongest neural baseline. Ablation studies on the fixed-point iterations and detailed error decomposition further confirm that PSTO achieves both high one-step accuracy and long-term stability in coupled rollouts. Time-step sensitivity analysis shows that PSTO maintains accuracy even with a tenfold larger time step, whereas baseline accuracies decay rapidly as the time step increases. This framework enables efficient, modular modeling of multiscale CDR dynamics by separating transport learning from the treatment of local kinetics.

title: NIMIS: A Structure-Agnostic, Chemically Informed Slot-Attention Framework for Demixing 1D $^1$H-NMR Mixture Spectra
abstract: The products of chemical reactions are usually complex mixtures that must be separated into their components before interpretable $^1$H-NMR spectra can be obtained. Direct analysis of the spectra of crude mixtures would accelerate reaction analysis and facilitate the exploration of new chemical space. We present NIMIS, a structure-agnostic, attention-based deep learning framework that groups the peaks of a 1D $^1$H-NMR mixture spectrum according to the component from which they originate. J-coupling information is introduced directly into the attention mechanism of a multi-head Transformer encoder, and the resulting contextualised peak embeddings are separated into components by slot attention. NIMIS was trained on 158,005 synthetic mixtures constructed from experimental spectra in the NMRexp database, covering molecules of up to 20 heavy atoms composed of C, H, N, O, S, F, Cl, Br and I. On held-out molecules it reaches a peak-to-component assignment accuracy of 82.28% for noise-free input and 77.34% with 10% integral noise, with a mean NIMIS score of 0.83 for correct assignments. NIMIS outperforms a conventional Transformer and simple baselines, and its performance carries over to a scaffold-disjoint evaluation. By grouping peaks into component-level sets, NIMIS provides a foundation for more robust mixture analysis methods, including methods capable of handling overlapping signals.

title: A Three-Motif-Based One-Dimensional Covalent Organic Framework as an Efficient Cathode Material for Stable Rechargeable Sodium-Ion Batteries
abstract: Crystalline one-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (1D COFs) hold great promise for diverse applications; however, their synthesis remains challenging, as it requires simultaneous control over chain dimensionality and crystallization of polymeric chains that are intrinsically prone to entanglement. Here, we show that benzo[1,2-b:4,5-b′]difuran-2,6(3H,7H)-dione (BDFO), in the presence of isoquinoline, effectively compels the trifunctional monomer 2,4,6-tris(4-formylphenyl)-1,3,5-triazine (TPFT) to polymerize as a V-shaped ditopic linker, affording 1D zigzag chains that stack in a…
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Partial Irreversibility During Electrochemical Lithiation of Iron Oxide Nanoparticle Arrays
abstract: Spinel iron oxides such as magnetite and maghemite are widely investigated as naturally abundant electrode materials for lithiation processes, with the challenge of the conversion process involving large volumetric changes leading to structural degradation. Here, we focus on the insertion stage to understand the reversibility of the involved intercalation process. Our thermodynamic approach employs voltammetry with nanostructured electrodes based on very small (ca. 13 nm) nanoparticles in an ordered array connected by conductive carbon.

title: Intelligent Imaging of Thermal Transport in Nanostructures
abstract: The ability to measure thermal properties and visualize heat transport processes with high spatial resolution is becoming increasingly important for materials discovery, next-generation electronics, and advanced manufacturing. As critical dimensions and architectures of novel materials and high performance electronics shrink and become more heterogeneous, thermal transport is no longer governed by bulk material properties alone, but by local variations in microstructure, such as interfaces and defects, while the operating conditions can also play a role. With the development of non-contact pump-probe thermoreflectance techniques, specific heat, thermal conductivity, and interface conductance can be mapped either through wide-field thermos-reflectance images or by scanning technique. However, key challenges remain such as the balance between imaging throughput and measurement accuracy, the extraction of multiple parameters with high confidence, and non-intrusive subsurface characterization, etc. This Review highlights recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI)-assistance in high-throughput data processing, visualizing interfacial thermal transport, and nonintrusive subsurface analysis, and offers outlooks for future research directions such as spectral mapping of heat carriers, three-dimensional property mapping, and AI-agentic experimental designs. We anticipate this Review will motivate future efforts in combining AI with experimental techniques to achieve unprecedented capabilities for thermal characterization of nanoscale materials and device characterization, facilitating materials discovery and electronics revolution.

title: Field-free deterministic spin-orbit torque magnetization switching using monolayer WTe2
abstract: An important step towards the practical implementation of spin-orbit torque magnetic memory is the field-free switching of the magnetization vector. In this work, we investigate spin-orbit torque-driven magnetization dynamics and switching devices comprising monolayer $\mathrm{WTe}_2$ as the spin-source material. We perform a comparative analysis of the two phases of $\mathrm{WTe}_2$, namely the $1\mathrm{T}_d$ and $1\mathrm{T}'$ with the necessary symmetries for field-free deterministic magnetization switching. We demonstrate switching in both systems and analyse the dependence of the switching dynamics on the applied bias voltage, ribbon orientation and width of the magnetic layer. Modelling the ferromagnet as an exchange-coupled macrospin within a non-equilibrium Green's function framework, we find that the $x$-ribbon geometry of the $1\mathrm{T}_d$ $\mathrm{WTe}_2$ phase generates a significantly larger current-induced spin polarization than the $1\mathrm{T}'$ phase, resulting in a larger damping-like torque on the adjacent magnetic layer and faster switching. The switching time of $1\mathrm{T}'$ devices varies strongly and non-monotonically with the width of the magnetic layer. In $1\mathrm{T}_d$ devices, it remains nearly constant over a broad range of widths, consistent with an edge-dominated torque. These results identify $x$-ribbon $1\mathrm{T}_d$-$\mathrm{WTe}_2$ as a promising spin source for field-free SOT-MRAM.

title: Probing thin films and their interfaces via angle-resolved second-harmonic generation
abstract: Increasing demands on the performance and reliability of optical thin films stimulate the development of more sensitive characterisation methods capable of investigating thin-film interfaces or local mechanical stress. Second-harmonic generation (SHG) is a phenomenon that can serve as a non-destructive probe, tracing local symmetry changes in the film surface, bulk, and buried interfaces. Here, we investigate the decomposition of the SHG response from these three regions by combining angle- and polarisation-resolved measurements. We utilised a theoretical model of SHG accounting for multiple reflections and optical interference in a thin layer. The theory was first experimentally evaluated using Ta2O5 films deposited on different glass substrates. The fitting procedure accurately reproduced the measured SHG responses, revealing pronounced substrate-dependent variations in the buried-interface contribution, while the surface and effective-bulk responses remained similar. As the next step, we studied the reliability of the SHG signal decomposition into the surface, bulk and buried-interface components. The decomposition was evaluated by generating synthetic datasets and testing whether their retrieval was unique and accurate. The influence of film thickness, measurement noise, uncertainties in linear-optical parameters, and the polarisation channels used on the retrieval of nonlinear susceptibilities was also examined. Our results demonstrate that reliable separation of SHG contributions requires accurate linear optical parameters, global fitting of multiple polarisation channels, and sufficiently pronounced interference features, outlining the capabilities and practical limitations of SHG-based region-specific characterisation of optical thin films.

title: How to Effectively Manage the Energy in Residential Systems: Development and Comparison of Methods
abstract: The transition from fossil fuels presents significant challenges in energy management. To ensure a sustainable energy future, it is crucial to reduce energy consumption when possible and to synchronize electricity consumption and storage with the production from sources with low greenhouse gas emissions. This thesis explores a variety of energy management methods used to manage batteries, heat pumps, and other energy-related systems. The thesis presents three simulation cases alongside one real-world experiment to compare energy management done through simple rules, optimization, and machine learning methods. Furthermore, this thesis introduces TreeC, a novel machine learning-based method that learns understandable yet efficient energy management strategies, applicable to many cases. The three key contributions of this thesis can be summarized as follows: 1) The developed TreeC method demonstrates competitive performance compared to a variety of energy management approaches, such as model predictive control and reinforcement learning, across a diverse set of energy management problems. The understandability of TreeC's energy management strategies greatly improves the transparency and trustworthiness of machine learning-based energy management. 2) The real-world experiment highlights the need to validate energy management methods on actual hardware and not solely on simulations. Both TreeC and model predictive control performed worse than in simulations, due to, respectively, insufficiently representative training data and the real-time input data not being reliable enough. 3) Energy management algorithms reduce costs in electrified Belgian dwellings, particularly in poorly insulated dwellings, electric vehicle chargers, and photovoltaic installations. However, on average, these cost savings do not yet outweigh the current costs and effort required to implement such algorithms.

title: Ab-initio study of magnetic interaction in RNiO2: role of rare-earth size and epitaxial strain
abstract: In this paper we present a systematic first-principles investigation of the structure and nearest-neighbor magnetic exchange interactions in the infinite-layer RNiO2 thin-film series (R = La-Lu), under the constrain of different substrates. Density functional theory calculations are first employed to optimize the crystal structures, while CAS+DDCI correlated wave-function calculations were used for the determination of the magnetic exchanges. This methodology allows to obtain magnetic interactions in good agreement with RIXS experimental estimations. In the pristine case, our results confirm that the structure of RNiO2 (except for R = La and Ce) adopts the I4/mcm space group, characterized by an out-of-plane rotation of the NiO4 plaquettes. This result remains valid under substrate constrains, even if compressive strain reduces the amplitude of the rotational distortion and leads to an enhancement of the magnetic exchange interaction relative to the pristine structures. The latter are found to depend sensitively on both the rare-earth ionic radius and the applied epitaxial strain. These results highlight the role of structural distortions and substrate-induced strain in tuning magnetic interactions in infinite-layer nickelates.

title: FamilySpace: From Emergent Chemical Semantics to Controllable Crystal Generation
abstract: Latent crystal generative models typically combine a variational autoencoder (VAE) for learning atom-wise representations with a flow model that transports a simple source distribution to the learned latent distribution. However, previous studies have mainly focused on the quality of generated crystals, leaving the structure and generative utility of the atom-wise latent space largely unexplored. In this work, we show that even a vanilla crystal VAE implicitly organizes atom-wise latent representations according to elemental families, with different families occupying largely separated regions of the latent space. We term this phenomenon emergent chemical semantics. This structure suggests that sampling from a family-specific latent region can bias the decoder toward atoms from the corresponding elemental family. Building on this insight, we propose FamilySpace, a framework for controlling the elemental-family composition of generated crystals. FamilySpace assigns each elemental family a distinct source component, forming a family-indexed multi-source distribution, and trains a flow model using source-target pairs matched by family. In inference, a user-specified family template selects the source component for each atom-wise representation, enabling direct control over the family composition of generated crystals. Experiments on MP-20 and MPTS-52 show that FamilySpace achieves competitive crystal-generation performance while matching prescribed elemental-family compositions. Moreover, selected family templates increase the fraction of generated crystals predicted to be stable or metastable, demonstrating that latent-space composition control can support targeted exploration of promising chemical regions without additional optimization techniques such as reinforcement learning. Code is available at https://github.com/hhw11/FamilySpace

title: Origin and hole-density dependence of the intrinsic spin Hall conductivity in inorganic halide perovskites
abstract: Metal halide perovskites have spin-orbit coupling among the strongest in semiconductors, yet whether their centrosymmetric bulk phases can convert charge current into spin current, and what controls the response, is unknown. Here we identify, from first-principles calculations on the four all-inorganic compounds CsBX3 (B = Pb, Sn; X = Br, I), the factors that govern their intrinsic spin Hall conductivity. The conductivity arises from the spin Berry curvature of the spin-orbit-split halide-p bands, 1.1-2.6 eV below the valence band maximum, and exceeds that of III-V and group-IV semiconductors when the Fermi level lies inside them. Because the valence band maximum is an s-p singlet, shifted only in second order, these contributions cancel in the undoped compounds, which respond like conventional semiconductors. With hole doping the response recovers, and at densities reachable by electric double-layer gating CsPbI3 attains the spin Hall conductivity of p-GaAs. The response is therefore determined by the position of the halide-p bands relative to the valence band maximum, not by the atomic spin-orbit constant, a criterion that applies to any semiconductor with an orbital-singlet band edge. These results point to CsPbI3 as a candidate gate-controlled source of spin current for perovskite spin-orbit torque devices.

title: Machine Learning-Enhanced Vibrational Spectroscopy for Mammalian Wildlife: A Critical Review of Conservation and Forensic Applications
abstract: Mammalian species differ in the biochemical composition of their tissues and fluids-subtle but statistically discriminable variation that vibrational spectroscopy can detect and machine learning can decode for applications spanning forensic investigation, conservation monitoring, and physiological assessment. This review critically examines machine learning applications across near-infrared (NIR), mid-infrared (MIR/FTIR), and Raman spectroscopy specifically for mammalian wildlife samples.

title: Monoclonal antibodies for detecting collagen IV α3α4α5 in basement membranes
abstract: The collagen IV 345 trimer forms a specialised network within basement membranes that is essential for normal kidney, inner ear and ocular function. Variants in COL4A3, COL4A4 or COL4A5 disrupt this network and cause Alport syndrome. Yet, current antibody tools detect individual collagen IV chains rather than the assembled 345 trimer. Here, we generated a recombinant human mini-COL4A345 trimer and used it to produce mouse monoclonal antibodies that recognise native collagen IV 345. We screened hybridomas using biolayer interferometry, native dot blotting, denaturing western blotting and immunofluorescence, followed by characterisation of selected purified antibodies using surface plasmon resonance. Three clones, Ms5, Ms44 and Ms72, detected native, folded collagen IV 345. We validated antibody specificity using Col4a3, Col4a5 and Col4a6 knockout mouse tissues, and assessed their utility for human kidney immunofluorescence and immunoprecipitation from mouse kidney. The antibodies detected conformationally intact collagen IV 345 in tissue, with no detectable cross-reactivity with collagen IV 112 or 556 networks under the conditions tested. Clone Ms72 provided the strongest and most consistent tissue signal, localising collagen IV 345 to the glomerular basement membrane, cochlear basement membranes and retinal pigment epithelium-associated basement membrane. Ms72 also immunoprecipitated endogenous collagen IV 3, 4 and 5 from wild-type kidney tissue, confirming recognition of the native complex. These monoclonal antibodies provide a resource for detecting collagen IV 345 in basement membrane networks. Their potential applications include assessment of the 345 heterotrimer in patient biopsies and evaluation of gene therapies and other interventions aimed at modulating 345 deposition in Alport syndrome.

title: Artificial intelligence tools for generating multimodal intensive care unit journey and discharge summaries: a scoping review
abstract: ObjectiveTo map and synthesise existing evidence on computational summarisation technologies, including machine learning-based and natural language processing-based approaches, designed to generate multimodal (textual, visual, and audio) patient summaries of adult intensive care unit (ICU) stays.Materials and methodsThis scoping review followed Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidance. Studies involving adults in any ICU setting and using artificial intelligence-enabled approaches to generate patient summaries were eligible.

title: New metal-organic material combines metallic conductivity with promise for light-sensing electronics
abstract: In modern electronics and computing, finding advanced materials that can efficiently move electrical charges without losing energy remains a critical scientific challenge. While traditional metals conduct electricity exceptionally well, researchers continually seek innovative hybrid materials that combine the design flexibility of chemistry with true metallic performance.

title: Comparative First-Principles Study of the Physical Properties, Phonon-Mediated Superconductivity and Functional Potential of Technetium-Based Binary Borides TcB2, Tc2B and Tc3B
abstract: Phonon-mediated superconductivity in binary transition-metal borides reflects a balance between the metal d-states, metal-boron bonding, and the lattice vibrations that couple to them. Here, we compare P6/mmm TcB2 at 20 GPa with I4/mcm Tc2B and P4/mmm Tc3B at 0 GPa within a first-principles framework. Their mechanical responses differ appreciably: TcB2 is the most rigid under its compressed condition, Tc2B shows the strongest tendency toward ductility, and Tc3B falls between the two. Despite these differences, all three phases remain metallic. The states at the Fermi level are dominated by Tc-4d character, although the extent of Tc-d/B-p mixing varies from one compound to another. Charge redistribution is more directional and B-centered in TcB2, but more delocalized around the Tc network in Tc2B and Tc3B. Inclusion of spin-orbit coupling leaves all three compounds metallic. The optical response remains metallic and electric field polarization dependent, with substantial visible reflectivity and strong ultraviolet absorption. Low-frequency Tc rich vibrations dominate the electron-phonon coupling (EPC). With μ* = 0.10, the Tc values of TcB2, Tc2B, and Tc3B are 24.92, 11.07, and 15.12 K, respectively. Although Tc3B exhibits a higher electronic density of states at the Fermi level, N(EF), TcB2 couples most strongly to EPC-active low-frequency modes, showing that the superconducting hierarchy depends on electronic-phonon matching rather than DOS magnitude alone.

title: Scattering Circular Dichroism from Spatially Modulated Anisotropic Magnetic Dipoles in BiFeO$_3$
abstract: Antiferromagnets with broken time-reversal symmetry, including altermagnets, have attracted growing interest because they can exhibit ferromagnet-like responses, such as the anomalous Hall effect and magneto-optical effects, despite their compensated spin structures. Such time-reversal symmetry breaking is characterized by ferroic time-reversal-odd multipoles, distinct from the conventional spin and orbital moments. Among them, the anisotropic magnetic dipole (AMD), which reflects the local orbital anisotropy, shares the symmetry of magnetization and can have a ferroic component even when the spin moments cancel. AMD responses have thus far been identified primarily in antiferromagnets with unit-cell magnetic periodicity, whereas spatially modulated AMDs in long-wavelength magnetic textures remain unexplored. Here, we report resonant soft x-ray small-angle scattering measurements on the antiferromagnetic spin cycloid of the multiferroic BiFeO$_3$. We observe pronounced circular dichroism in the resonant scattering intensity, i.e., scattering circular dichroism, which is not expected from the established cycloidal and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya-interaction-induced sinusoidal spin structures. We show that the staggered rotation of the FeO$_6$ octahedra gives rise to ferroic AMD components despite the antiparallel spin alignment. As the local magnetic symmetry varies with the cycloidal phase, these AMDs are spatially modulated and produce the dichroism through interference with the sinusoidal spin component. Our findings demonstrate that long-wavelength antiferromagnetic textures can host spatially modulated AMDs, opening new avenues for exploring hidden multipole textures in magnetic and multiferroic materials.

title: Design and Evaluation of Epira: An Automated Interview System for Case Investigation and Contact Tracing
abstract: Objective: Case investigation and contact tracing are labor-intensive. Web forms struggle when respondents need clarification before disclosing contacts, and open-ended chatbots may deviate from protocols. We developed and evaluated Epira, a protocol-controlled large language model (LLM) interviewer for multi-disease case investigation and contact tracing. Materials and Methods: Epira pairs LLM dialogue with a rule-based controller enforcing required questions, safety handoffs, and a structured case record, and adapts to new diseases by questionnaire upload. Local (Qwen2.5) and cloud (GPT-5.4) backends were tested. Study 1 used 108 simulated cases with ground-truth fields and contacts for measles and gonorrhea under Epira and open-ended conditions (864 sessions). Study 2 enrolled 72 volunteers in a 2$\times$2 disease-by-model interview assessing completion, usability, acceptability, and trust. Results: Across Study 1, Epira with a local LLM captured 88.9% of required fields and 60.1% of ground-truth contacts. Open-ended interviewers recovered 31.1-41.9 percentage points fewer required fields than the same models in Epira. In Study 2, completion was 100%; mean adapted System Usability Scale (SUS) was 82.95 $\pm$ 16.17 on a 0-100 scale and mean trust was 3.85 $\pm$ 0.77 on a 1-5 scale. Discussion: Protocol control drove completeness more than model choice. Local and cloud deployments produced similar records, supporting privacy-preserving local use with human review of routed interviews and missed contacts. Conclusion: Epira recovers required fields and contacts under diverse disclosure conditions, works with local and cloud LLMs, and received favorable usability and trust ratings.

title: An Explainable and Scalable Hierarchical Tensor Framework for Integrating Multi-Omics and Digital Pathomics
abstract: Background: Precision oncology requires integration of heterogeneous molecular and pathology data, yet many fusion models offer limited biologically grounded interpretability and struggle with missing modalities. Methods: We present Hierarchical Interpretable Tensor Fusion (HIT-Fuse), integrating six modalities: somatic copy number variation, DNA methylation, RNA sequencing, microRNA expression, RPPA protein abundance, and vision transformer-derived pathomics across four TCGA cohorts (glioma, lung adenocarcinoma, breast, and kidney cancer). Modality-specific autoencoders compress high-dimensional inputs, followed by two-stage CP tensor decomposition. Missing latent modalities are reconstructed using clinical covariates and observed omics to expand cohorts and retrain downstream models. A mathematical traceback mechanism enables global and local xAI attributions. Results: HIT-Fuse identifies distinct latent subgroups with significant survival stratification in glioma, breast, and kidney cohorts, both with complete and reconstructed modalities. Cohort expansion yields cohort-specific gains, including a 56.4% relative increase in weighted F1 for glioma. Biological validation against DepMap CRISPR screens, miRTarBase and RPPA annotations supports decoded drivers across all four cohorts. Essential gene rates range from 6.2% in glioma to 7.6% in lung cancer; example drivers include ANAPC11, SNRPD1, PLK1 and RPL14. Of decoded miRNAs, 71-92% have miRTarBase regulatory support, while 77-84% of selected genes are covered in DepMap. Conclusions: HIT-Fuse combines hierarchical tensor fusion, missing-modality reconstruction and traceable attributions to support interpretable multi-omics and digital pathology-based cancer prognosis across heterogeneous cohorts.

title: Fractional Charge at Dislocations from Band-Inversion Cancellation
abstract: Band inversions with opposite Chern numbers cancel in the Hall response and yield counterpropagating boundary modes that can gap out. However, a bulk probe of the topology that survives such a cancellation is lacking. We here show that dislocations in inversion-symmetric two-band crystals with cancelling band inversions bind a half-integer charge, which reveals the quantized bulk polarization of the bond-centered obstructed atomic limit realized by such crystals. To demonstrate this, we continuously deform a broad class of two-band lattice models into decoupled chains, without closing the bulk gap or breaking the inversion symmetry, where the dislocation charge follows from a count of occupied bonds. Notably, the fractional part of this charge is insensitive to local perturbations of the dislocation core, and it therefore persists after the in-gap core state is removed, as we show analytically in the chain limit and numerically away from it. In the Weyl-semimetal counterpart, the response to a magnetic flux separates this crystalline charge from the charge set by the Chern number of each momentum slice. We propose that a half-integer core charge that persists after the in-gap peak disappears from the local spectrum can be detected in artificial electronic and optical lattices, with metamaterials providing complementary access to the core modes.

title: Surrogate Verifiers Shape Decisions in Closed-Loop Experimental Design
abstract: High throughput, automated screening has revolutionized biological experimentation and prompted predictions of AI-enabled "self-driving" labs. Deployed autonomous lab systems typically use a learned surrogate to predict new experimental candidates and rank which conditions deserve expensive follow-up. Determining whether a computational surrogate verifier can substitute for an experimental assay's ground truth requires an understanding of model accuracy, uncertainty, and extrapolation. In this work, we present surrogate verifiers trained on N=7,688 Lacticaseibacillus growth curves exploring a 10-dimensional media component experimental design space. We train surrogate models across six distinct families including polynomial, Gaussian-process, tree-ensemble, neural, and Monod-kinetic forms to predict maximum optical density (OD600). Surrogates ranked by the most commonly reported accuracy metrics (held-out R^2; MAE; RMSE) disagree sharply on which experiments to test next and the best achievable yield. We evaluate models in a Bayesian optimization loop and find that the model used as the active learning oracle matters more than the acquisition function or batch size. We apply conformal calibration to build a model-agnostic assessment criterion of uncertainty and model coverage. We end by evaluating model accuracy and calibration under transfer to an unseen related bacterial strain, and confirm on a prospective validation plate that the transferred verifier's intervals fail in the direction and region our retrospective analysis predicts. This work explores the surrogate verifier within the loop as a previously underexplored axis of closed-loop design and points towards best calibration practices.

title: Investigating the critical role of serine in antimicrobial peptide binding to lipopolysaccharide
abstract: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a major component of the Gram-negative bacterial outer membrane, is a potent endotoxin responsible for triggering severe host immune responses and sepsis. Understanding the atomic-level mechanisms governing how antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) recognize and neutralize LPS is essential for designing effective anti-endotoxin therapeutics. Here, we present an in silico investigation of the single-molecule interaction between Escherichia coli O111:B4 LPS and the cationic antimicrobial peptide GL13K, alongside two single-point mutants at position 9 (GL13KS9A and GL13KS9T), using all-atom molecular dynamics and umbrella sampling simulations. Consistent with experimental trends, mutating SER9 into alanine significantly alters peptide binding affinity to LPS. Surpisingly, removal of the polar character of serine leads to substantial changes in the interaction of the N-terminus with LPS via the loss of hydrogen bonding to stabilize a hook shape at the C-terminal end. In specific, while wild-type GL13K exhibits the strongest unbinding free-energy barrier, the S9A substitution changes the conformational landscape in such a way as to redirect the peptide's N-terminus from lipid A toward the core oligosaccharide and substantially reduces the unbinding barrier, whereas S9T maintains an similar affinity. Our work demonstrates the effects of distal mutations even in peptides on their binding and lays important groundwork for the development of peptide-based LPS inhibitors.

title: Glycoform Distributions and Heparan Sulfate Binding of Intact SARS-CoV-2 Spike Variants by DIA-ECCR Native Mass Spectrometry
abstract: Glycosylation influences the structure, immunogenicity, and evolutionary selection of the SARS CoV 2 spike protein (S), but its extensive heterogeneity has hindered characterization of intact glycoform distributions. Here, we illustrate a data-independent analysis - electron capture charge reduction (DIA-ECCR) native mass spectrometry workflow for direct analysis of intact spike glycoforms across multiple variants. DIA-ECCR resolves variant-dependent differences in glycoform distributions and higher mass subpopulations. Monte Carlo simulations based on published site-specific bottom-up glycoproteomic data reproduce the central mass of the D614G experimental distribution and support a connection between intact and bottom-up measurements, while the broader experimental distributions and a second Gamma subpopulation indicate heterogeneity not captured by the simulations Mass photometry and charge detection mass spectrometry provide orthogonal measurements consistent with the DIA-ECCR results. DIA-ECCR also resolves mass shifts associated with binding of truncated heparan sulfate, demonstrating analysis of a heterogeneous protein:ligand complex. Together, these results outline a practical workflow that combines DIA-ECCR with native mass spectrometry (nMS) for characterizing intact glycoform distributions and ligand binding in highly heterogeneous glycoprotein assemblies, with potential applications in antigen characterization, vaccine design, and biopharmaceutical quality control.

title: Structure of CPC-PP2A(B56) Kinase-Phosphatase Signaling Hub in Chromosome Segregation Fidelity
abstract: Accurate chromosome segregation relies on kinase-phosphatase crosstalk that controls protein interactions underpinning sister chromatid cohesion, error correction and timely anaphase onset. The PP2A(B56) phosphatase and the Aurora B kinase-containing Chromosomal Passenger Complex (CPC), two central mitotic regulators, are independently recruited to centromeres by Shugoshin1 (Sgo1). Here, using biochemical reconstitutions and cryo-electron microscopy, we show that PP2A(B56) and CPC form an integrated signaling platform independent of Sgo1. The CPC binds PP2A(B56) directly through two Borealin elements: a previously uncharacterized LxxIxE-like motif and the dimerization domain. Sgo1 selectively remodels the dimerization-domain interface, while the LxxIxE-like motif sustains PP2A(B56)-CPC association. Disrupting this interaction increases chromosome segregation errors, compromising segregation fidelity. Our findings reveal a direct kinase-phosphatase association as an additional layer of mitotic regulation that safeguards segregation fidelity.

title: Integrated analysis of laser-captured glomerular proteome characterizes the expression and functional role of APOE in membranous nephropathy
abstract: Background MN is a prevalent primary glomerular disease causing adult nephrotic syndrome. Clinically, invasive renal biopsy acts as the pathological gold standard, while the widely used serological anti-PLA2R antibody has limited sensitivity and cannot reflect glomerular lesion severity. Conventional immunosuppressive regimens face frequent drug resistance and relapse, and core tissue-derived pathogenic regulators remain poorly defined.

title: Evaluation of sources of variability in a TEER (trans-epithelial/endothelial electrical resistance) system
abstract: Trans-epithelial/endothelial electrical resistance (TEER) measurements are a key nondestructive measurement of the barrier integrity of cells grown on inserts. To support the use of TEER measurements in bioassays, we have evaluated the sources of variability in a case study involving a chamber-based TEER system to assess a gut co-culture model. Data from 23 separate experiments, each lasting 22 d, were evaluated. Multiple lines of evidence suggested minimal variability within a run, a period during which several plates were analyzed sequentially. In contrast, run-to-run variability was substantially larger, even when two runs were performed several hours apart on the same day. Bayesian analysis of both KCl and blank insert data revealed that run-to-run variability was among the largest sources of variability, with relative uncertainty values of 3 % to 6 % of the mean value. Correlational analysis investigated whether deviations of KCl or blank insert TEER values within a run compared to long-term median values were correlated with deviations of the biculture gut model values within that same run from their long-term median values. Unexpectedly, the KCl values were not correlated, while the blank insert values had a weak correlation. We also evaluated the information gained from different control measurements. The findings from this study can influence how statistical analyses are performed on TEER results and can inform the design of robust TEER methods. For example, the approaches described here can be used to characterize variability within and among runs in TEER measurements for other methods.

title: Constitutive Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Finite Element Model Updating: Closed-Form Hyperelastic Strain Energies from Heterogeneous Experiments
abstract: Calibrating a hyperelastic constitutive model for a soft material traditionally poses two problems: an expert must choose its functional form, and several homogeneous tests must determine its parameters. Neural constitutive models solve the first, but either remain black boxes or draw on a library of candidate terms fixed in advance. Full-field measurements, such as those from digital image correlation (DIC), promise to solve the second, replacing those tests by a single heterogeneous one. Two gaps remain: flexibility during training with interpretability afterwards, and a way to train such a model on one heterogeneous test. Here we close both. We embed a constitutive Kolmogorov-Arnold network (CKAN) in finite element model updating (FEMU) and train it by minimizing the mismatch between the predicted and the measured kinematic fields and reaction forces. Pruning and symbolic regression then reduce the trained network to a compact closed-form strain energy that satisfies every constitutive requirement. On perforated natural-rubber membranes, the CKANs reproduce the DIC displacement fields with median errors between one and two percent, and transfer to a hole pattern withheld from training. On a perforated silicone plate, a CKAN trained on one stretch profile at a single load reproduces that profile and the measured reaction force to within a few percent. On an aortic specimen inflated under pressure, an anisotropic CKAN predicts the inflated three-dimensional shape. The discovered closed-form energies match the CKANs they replace on the training data and can be compared directly with established models.

title: Emergent Fatigue Dynamics from Foundational Interatomic Potentials
abstract: Foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials are trained on large, diverse DFT datasets, but their validation rests on equilibrium states, which does not guarantee correct emergent behavior in large-scale molecular dynamics. Where no direct experimental validation is available, comparisons to physically motivated potentials are valuable for drawing insight. We distinguish static properties, which are thermally accessible, from emergent properties, which require work from an external fatigue stress to drive rare events, and compare the potentials on both. An EAM potential and the NequIP foundational potential both agree closely with reference data for many near-equilibrium properties, but NequIP predicts an anomalously low intrinsic stacking fault energy ($\sim7$ times lower than EAM) and thus predicts far more plastic deformation under fatigue cycling of a nanoscale flaw modeled after the classical Griffith crack problem. Per-atom energy distributions after loading show that the two potentials differ most at energies far above what is thermally accessible. We also document memory-related crashes and silent extrapolation as practical concerns for practitioners of these foundational model forms.

title: Unexpected properties of nucleotide condensates could facilitate the RNA world
abstract: A key question in the RNA world hypothesis for the origin of life is the nature of the compartment that separates and protects the RNA from its environment. While membranes are a leading candidate for the initial compartment, biomolecular condensates have been proposed as an alternative, possibly simpler route to compartments. Here we show that bona fide liquid condensates form spontaneously when nucleotides (such as ATP) are mixed with divalent cations and a short-chain alcohol or diol in water. These condensates do not require any polymer to form, but can concentrate polymers like RNA and DNA, which show unexpected chemical behavior inside the condensates. Most surprisingly, RNA survives for days inside nucleotide condensates under acidic conditions that cause rapid and extensive hydrolysis in bulk. This effect is also observed for a phosphate-ester model substrate and therefore likely reflects the suppression of backbone cleavage. Coarse-grained simulations suggest that the condensate interior is bound together by magnesium-phosphate bridging interactions and is therefore highly depleted of water. At neutral pH, the same compartment reverses the course of a hammerhead ribozyme reaction, shifting it from cleavage toward religation. Finally, we observe that nucleotide droplets also spontaneously organize phospholipids at their surface, suggesting a possible evolutionary route from biomolecular condensates toward membranes. Thus, we believe that nucleotide condensates, which are built from the same building blocks as the genetic polymers themselves, overcome long-standing challenges with the RNA world hypothesis for the origin of life by protecting nucleic acids and reshaping their chemistry.

title: Actinium-225 Pretargeted Radioimmunotherapy against Colorectal Cancer using Self-Assembling and Disassembling Antibodies
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer deaths worldwide. GPA33, expressed on 95% of CRC, has been extensively targeted by IgG-attached payloads in conventional radioimmunotherapy (RIT), but toxicity was dose-limiting. A 2-step pretargeted radioimmunotherapy (PRIT) regimen using Self-Assembling-Disassembling antibody (SADA) specific for GPA33 (10 mg/kg) intravenous (IV) in step #1 and 24 h later [86Y]Y-ABD (9 nmole) IV in step #2, avoided normal gut uptake in non-human primates.

title: Scalable electron tomography for connectomics.
abstract: We demonstrate limited-tilt, serial-section electron tomography (ET), which can non-destructively map brain circuits over large 3D volumes and provide high-resolution, supramolecular details within subvolumes of interest. Here we show accelerated ET imaging of semi-thick sections ( >500 nm) from the mouse cerebellar cortex, with 3D resolution <15 nm and machine learning-based image augmentation, providing the capacity to resolve key features of neuronal circuits including chemical synapses, endocytic structures and gap junctions.

title: Catalytic Activation of “Orbital-Symmetry-Forbidden” Pericyclic Reactions
abstract: Conservation of orbital symmetry imposes high barriers on formally forbidden pericyclic reactions, rendering such transformations inaccessible regardless of their thermodynamic driving force. A particularly compelling subset of such reactions involves the conversion of high-energy photoisomers. Although the catalytic activation of these and related orbital-symmetry-forbidden transformations has attracted increasing interest, the mechanistic understanding of how chemically different types of catalysts overcome orbital symmetry constraints has remained elusive.

title: A generative neural network architecture for structure elucidation
abstract: Determining molecular structure is central to chemistry. One-dimensional (1D) 1H and 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is a standard technique in small molecule structure determination, but deducing a structure from these spectra remains challenging because of the vast chemical space involved. Deep learning models that predict structures directly from NMR data have shown potential in navigating this space, but are trained largely on simulated spectra and perform poorly on real experimental data.

title: Natural fiber based natural rubber hybrid composites: Prospects and applications
abstract: Natural rubber (NR), derived from the Hevea brasiliensis tree, commonly referred to as the rubber tree, has been a crucial component in various industries for decades. The remarkable properties of NR, including its high elasticity, resilience, and exceptional mechanical strength, make it indispensable in the production of tires, seals, gaskets, medical equipment, and numerous other products. However, the growing focus on environmental conservation and the increasing demand for sustainable resources have increased interest in eco-friendly alternatives.

title: Benchmarking and Discovery of Ligands for Sterically Challenging Copper-Catalyzed C–N Cross-Couplings
abstract: Cu-catalyzed C–N cross-coupling has emerged as an attractive alternative to Pd-catalyzed methods from a sustainability point of view, yet ligand performance across sterically demanding substrate classes remains poorly understood. Herein, we report a benchmarking study of seven state-of-the-art ligands across 30 aryl halides and two representative amines to systematically evaluate steric effects in Cu-catalyzed amination.

title: Thorium and Uranium bis - and tris -Tetraalkylphospholide Complexes
abstract: Phospholides are phosphorus-containing analogues of cyclopentadienides and softer p-donor ligands, but their actinide chemistry remains underdeveloped. We report the first thorium complexes of the tetraalkylphospholides TMP ({PC 4 Me 4 } – ) and TEP ({PC 4 Et 4 } – ): the tris(phospholide) complexes [Th IV (PC 4 R 4 ) 3 X] (R = Me, Et; X = Cl, Br), together with their uranium(IV) analogues [U IV (PC 4 R 4 ) 3 Cl].

title: (Arylsulfonyl)acetonitrile as an Efficient Unified Reagent for the Photocatalyzed Hydrosulfonylation of Alkenes
abstract: We report the organophotocatalyzed hydrosulfonylation of alkenes using (arylsulfonyl)acetonitriles (AACN) as a unified reagent acting both as a sulfonyl radical precursor, via photocatalytic C-S bond cleavage and as an intrinsic hydrogen-atom donor. This strategy expands the sulfonyl radical toolbox, offering broad substrate scope and enabling efficient synthesis of structurally diverse sulfones with excellent functional group tolerance.

title: Multiscale Modeling of Virus Capsid Self-Assembly Reveals How Small Molecule Antivirals Can Redirect Assembly Pathways and Products
abstract: Controlling the assembly of a virus capsid, a regular complex of hundreds of subunits, has applications for development of antivirals and for development of nanocontainers. Recent work has shown that a class of small molecules called capsid assembly modulators (CAMs) is promising for treating Hepatitis B virus (HBV). CAMs bind to HBV capsid proteins and alter their self-assembly, leading to nonfunctional and malformed structures. The mechanisms by which CAMs alter capsid assembly remain unclear. Here, we use a kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) model for HBV capsid assembly to simulate how CAMs affect this complex reaction. The model is parametrized from all-atom simulations, resulting in unprecedented correlation between simulation and biochemical and structural observations. Simulations reproduce the effect of CAMs on experimental assembly products and their distributions. By analyzing assembly trajectories, we clarify the roles of thermodynamics and kinetics in determining assembly products, identify assembly mechanisms, and predict the key intermediates that lead to either capsids or malformed structures. Our findings enhance our fundamental understanding of capsid assembly, help advance the development of CAMs as a treatment for HBV and, more broadly, inform efforts to direct self-assembly pathways toward specific products.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Nonheme Fe Enzyme-Catalyzed Enantioselective and Regiodivergent C(sp3)-H Amidation: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Synthesis of 1,2- and 1,3-Diamine Derivatives
abstract: Nonheme Fe enzyme-catalyzed asymmetric, site-selective C-H amidation remains underexplored. Here we report the repurposing and directed evolution of the plant-derived nonheme Fe enzyme 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid oxidase (ACCO) into a family of biocatalysts for highly regio- and enantioselective C(sp3)-H amidation. Engineered ACCO variants catalyzed the asymmetric synthesis of cyclic ureas from N-(benzoyloxy)urea substrates, which are readily prepared from aliphatic amines, through the activation of benzylic, allylic, propargylic, and unactivated aliphatic C(sp3)-H bonds, including enantioconvergent amidation of racemic tertiary C(sp3)-H substrates. Directed evolution further generated complementary enzymes that selectively promoted either 1,5- or 1,6-hydrogen atom transfer, enabling catalyst-controlled, regiodivergent enantioselective synthesis of both 1,2- and 1,3-diamine derivatives from common precursors. The evolved biocatalysts exhibited total turnover numbers of up to 4,500 and were readily applicable to gram-scale whole-cell biotransformations. Mechanistic investigations supported a stepwise mechanism involving a carbon-centered radical intermediate. Kinetic isotope effect and isotopically labeled substrate studies indicated C(sp3)-H bond cleavage as the rate-limiting step, while stereochemical analyses revealed that the overall enantioselectivity is determined by the C-N bond-forming radical rebound rather than hydrogen atom transfer. These results established nonheme Fe enzymes as a versatile platform for selective C-H amidation and further expanded the scope of new-to-nature nonheme Fe biocatalysis for asymmetric C-H functionalization.

title: Quantification of cannabidiolic acid in Cannabis sativa using a two-component allosteric protein biosensor
abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD) is an important medicinal cannabinoid which accumulates in the Cannabis sativa plant as the precursor cannabidiolic acid (CBDA). Measurement of CBDA levels is important for crop valuation, harvest optimisation, and quality control. However, its quantification typically requires laboratory-based analytical methods that are not readily deployable at the point of need. Here, we report the development of an engineered protein biosensor for selective CBDA detection based on chemically induced dimerization of engineered nanobody domains. Here a cannabidiol-responsive nanobody pair was incorporated into a two-component beta-lactamase-based biosensor architecture, such that ligand binding ultimately results in reconstitution of beta-lactamase activity quantified in a simple colorimetric assay. The resulting sensor displayed high affinity for CBD (KD = 1.9 +/- 0.2 nM) and CBDA (KD = 32 +/- 4 nM). Structure analysis informed a single substitution mutation of ligand-binding nanobody to shift its selectivity in favour of CBDA. This minimal modification inverted sensor specificity, generating a CBDA-selective biosensor that showed no detectable activation either by CBD or the immediate biosynthetic precursor, cannabigerolic acid (CBGA). The engineered sensor exhibited nanomolar affinity for CBDA (KD = 21 +/- 2.4 nM), an 8.4-fold dynamic range, and a limit of detection of 0.5 nM. Sensor performance was validated using crude extracts from CBDA-producing biomass and achieved 95.6% agreement with LCMS-based quantification.

title: Population-scale identification of gut commensals that antagonize antibiotic-resistant pathogens.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance poses a global threat, yet microbiome-encoded defenses against antibiotic resistance gene (ARG)-associated pathogens remain poorly defined. Here, we analyze 12,238 human gut metagenomes and prioritize 159 commensal species ("coexcluders") that show inverse associations with ARG-associated pathogenic taxa. These taxa carry low ARG burdens and encode candidate antimicrobial peptide repertoires.

title: Successful high-purity synthesis of the challenging-to-produce cerium orthoferrite!
abstract: A research team including scientists from Ehime University successfully synthesized high-purity CeFeO3, a difficult-to-produce cerium–iron mixed oxide, using hydrogen reduction. By optimizing hydrogen concentration and gas flow rate, they achieved a phase purity of up to 99 mol%. The team also clarified the formation mechanism and identified factors that hinder synthesis. This method, published in the journal Inorganic Chemistry, provides a foundation for future research into applications in magnetic materials and catalysis.

title: FEA solver integration of a composite World Model with a Spiking Neural Network memory Block for computationally efficient modelling of defects and variabilities
abstract: Each fibre-reinforced composite structure has a unique material architecture. The manufacturing methods used and the presence of defects lead to local variations which require material-scale models that can resolve the response in real time at every location in the structure. Concurrent multi-scale schemes provide this capability, but at a prohibitive computational cost for large structures as the number of integration points and time increments scales with size. Surrogates have been studied extensively as replacements for material-scale models to mitigate these computational limitations.
