title: Topology-Enabled Self-Verification of Quantum Hall Resistance Standards
abstract: The scaling of multi-element quantized Hall array resistance standards necessitates rigorous validation that internal quantization has not broken down without relying on the verification of dissipationless edge state transport. One proposed solution is to use a Symmetric Precision Quantization Reliability criterion, a mathematical framework that statistically assures such validation strictly through outer terminal measurements of Cn-symmetric designs. This criterion essentially bounds the likelihood of hidden localized defects arising from quantum Hall breakdown and has potential uses in quantum computing and semiconductor testing but is presented in the context of its application toward quantum electrical standards.

title: Lattice dynamics study of (Bi1-xSbx)2Te3 compounds: Comparative compositional study of force constants and Grüneisen parameters
abstract: We performed a comprehensive Raman spectroscopy study of (Bi1-xSbx)2Te3 (BST-x) compounds, with varying Sb concentration, under ambient and high-pressure conditions. At ambient conditions, the frequency of all observed Raman-active modes (E1g, A11g, E2g, A21g) is blue-shifting with increasing Sb concentration, albeit with varying concentration-dependent rate. Based on these results, we calculated the relative force constants as a function of Sb concentration using a harmonic approximation, which shows a mode-dependent variation. The force constants for the lower frequency Raman modes (E1 g and A11g) remain almost composition-independent, while for the higher-frequency ones a profound softening (E2g) or stiffening (A21g) was determined. From the Raman spectroscopy measurements under high-pressure conditions, the corresponding Grüneisen parameters for the three observed Raman-active modes (A11g, E2g, A21g) as a function of composition were determined by combining them with the previously reported Equation of States and the corresponding bulk modulus B0 of the ambient-conditions R-3m phase. The average Grüneisen parameter exhibits a clear maximum for BST-07. Based on Slack's equation, these results are directly related to the optimal ZT values for this composition. Our study provides a solid framework for connecting composition, lattice dynamics, and thermal-transport behaviour, towards establishing the microscopic origin of thermoelectric optimization in BST compounds.

title: FrontierReplay: Split-Free Exact Prefix Caching for Hybrid Language Models
abstract: Hybrid language models combine self-attention with recurrent layers whose in-place state updates restrict prefix reuse to exact saved positions. Saving states on a coarse grid wastes reusable prefixes, whereas existing fine-grained exact caches must cut the prefill forward pass at each mid-prompt checkpoint, adding scheduler steps that outweigh the reuse gains under load. We observe that across multi-turn chat, agent loops, document question answering, and tree search, prefix reuse almost always ends at structural boundaries predictable in advance, such as turn ends and known branch points. We present FrontierReplay, a prefix caching system that materializes exact checkpoints at these boundaries without cutting the prefill. While the forward pass runs uncut, FrontierReplay logs a short window of recurrent-layer inputs and invokes a cross-layer, state-only replay kernel to build the target state 6-37x cheaper per token than full recomputation without host synchronization. A frontier-aware retention policy prioritizes active anchors and proven branches while lending dead checkpoint slots to the attention KV cache. Across diverse hybrid architectures, model scales, and workloads, FrontierReplay delivers clear gains over existing exact caches, lowering median time to first token (TTFT) by 16-89% (up to 8.9x), raising 80% service-level objective (SLO) capacity by up to 1.73x, and improving goodput by up to 4.26x (3.67x at larger scales). Compared with approximate replay methods, FrontierReplay delivers up to 1.54x higher goodput while preserving exact task accuracy, avoiding the up to 17% accuracy drop suffered by approximation on long contexts.

title: GPU-Accelerated Full Configuration Interaction for 1.7 Trillion Determinants
abstract: Full configuration interaction (FCI) accounts for all electronic correlation effects and provides an exact ground-state energy within a given basis set, serving as an accuracy benchmark for approximate quantum-chemical methods. However, its exponential execution time and memory requirement restrict its application to very small molecular systems. In this work, we present a distributed GPU-accelerated FCI implementation that extends the tractable determinant space and significantly reduces execution time. We successfully calculate the exact ground-state energy of NH2OH within the 6–31G basis set with 1.7 × 1012 determinants in 13.4 h on 1,024 GPUs, representing, to the best of our knowledge, the largest fully converged uncompressed FCI calculation reported to date. The implementation also achieves up to a 58-fold speedup compared with a CPU-based implementation (13-fold for the previously largest system with 1.3 × 1012 determinants). These advances facilitate the computation of exact reference energies, especially for strongly correlated systems, with applications in benchmarking of approximate methods. As an illustration, we calculate the FCI potential energy curve for N2/cc-pVDZ (10e, 26o) in 1.7 h, which shows that using HCI rather than exact FCI as the reference underestimates the error of the hybrid quantum–classical method by up to 20 mHa in the strongly correlated dissociation regime. The implementation also supports unequal numbers of α- and β-spin electrons, enabling open-shell calculations in nonzero-MS sectors. As an application, we obtain exact energies for the complete lowest-state spin ladder (S = 0–5) of the [Fe2S2(SCH3)4]2– CAS(30e, 20o) model, confirming a systematic deviation from a single-J bilinear Heisenberg description.
venue: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

title: 1,8-Azulenedicarboxylic Imides: Excited-State Properties and Catalytic Activity of a Nonalternant π-System
abstract: Imide-functionalized polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) represent an important class of π-conjugated molecules; however, their nonalternant isomers remain largely unexplored. Herein, we report the synthesis and investigation of the structural, photophysical, and excited-state properties of 1,8-azulenedicarboxylic imides as nonalternant isomers of 1,8-naphthalimides.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Mechanistic Insights into ADAR1-p110 Nuclear Import: A Dual-Interface Interaction with Transportin-1
abstract: The human ADAR1 exists as two isoforms: the predominantly cytoplasmic-localized p150, recognized for its role in suppression of aberrant immune activation, and the predominantly nuclear-localized p110 (missing the N terminal Z domain), whose biological functions remain less understood but are thought to rely heavily on its subcellular localization. Despite its structural similarity to the Z domain unique to ADAR1-p150, the functional significance of the Z{beta} domain shared by both isoforms remains unclear. Here, we identify an additional mechanism contributing to the nuclear import of ADAR1-p110 through a dual-interface interaction with transportin-1 (TNPO1), involving both the Z{beta} and dsRBD3 domains of ADAR1. Using cryo-electron microscopy, we show that Z{beta} engages TNPO1 at its canonical cargo-binding groove, while dsRBD3 binds at a peripheral site overlapping the RanGTP binding interface. Structure-guided mutagenesis and biochemical analyses support the contribution of Z{beta} to TNPO1 recognition. Disruption of the interaction between ADAR1 Z{beta} domain and TNPO1 alters the nucleocytoplasmic distribution of ADAR1-p110, resulting in increased cytoplasmic accumulation despite the retention of the previously characterized dsRBD3-associated nuclear localization signal. Furthermore, cytoplasmic redistribution of ADAR1-p110 mutants is accompanied by global suppression of cytosolic innate immune signaling pathways and reduced expression of interferon-stimulated genes. Together, these findings identify ADAR1 Z{beta} as an additional TNPO1-recognition element synergizing with dsRBD3 that contributes to ADAR1-p110 nuclear localization and highlight the relationship between its subcellular distribution and immune regulatory activity.

title: Conserved Vulnerability, Local Tunability: How Binding Proteins Read Ligand Fluorination
abstract: While rare in nature, fluorinated compounds are ubiquitous in synthetic chemicals ranging from pharmaceuticals to agrochemicals, yet how proteins recognize these anthropogenic molecules remains poorly understood. Here, we use three structurally and evolutionarily divergent solute-binding proteins (SBPs) specific for short-chain dicarboxylic acids as a comparative model system to dissect the principles governing protein-fluorocompound recognition. X-ray crystal structures reveal that each SBP uses a distinct binding mode, ranging from backbone-mediated to side-chain-dominated hydrogen bonding. Despite their structural divergence, ITC shows that all three proteins exhibit a conserved vulnerability upon binding perfluorinated ligands: binding affinity drops up to 80-fold, or is abolished, across all three proteins regardless of fold or binding mode. In contrast, sensitivity to partial fluorination is locally tunable, with one protein even binding a fluorinated ligand more tightly than its non-fluorinated counterpart. Using X-ray crystallography, molecular dynamics simulations, and site-directed mutagenesis, we show that aromatic residues positioned near the ligand contribute to this tunability, capable of either penalizing or favoring fluorinated ligands. Together, these findings establish that ligand-fluorination sensitivity reflects a conserved chemical vulnerability layered with locally tunable, structurally encoded selectivity, providing a roadmap for predicting and engineering protein recognition of fluorinated compounds.

title: Growth-law offset and efficient protein synthesis in fast-growing bacteria
abstract: Growth laws refer to simple relationships between various cellular components and the growth rate for exponentially growing bacteria subjected to various environmental and genetic perturbations. The best studied among these is the ribosomal growth law, which refers to a relationship between the ribosome content and the growth rate under different nutrient conditions. This relationship is affine, which means a linear dependence on the growth rate plus a constant offset. This offset, referred to here as the "growth-law offset" and which is substantial in size, has been rationalized in terms of ribosome sequestration and protein degradation effects in the slow growth regime. These effects however cannot account for the sizable offset observed at medium and fast growth, where the efficiency of protein synthesis is predominant. Here, we use a simple effective model of translation to show that efficient protein synthesis in the medium to fast-growth regime does in fact require a substantial growth-law offset, on the order of that observed in Escherichia coli. Our key observation is that efficient protein synthesis requires a nonlinear relationship between non-sequestered ribosomes and growth rate, but in the medium to fast-growth regime this relationship is well approximated by the affine relation in the growth law, with the offset being necessary for the efficient balance between ribosomal and non-ribosomal proteins directly involved in protein synthesis.

title: Crystal structure of the first de novo designed phosphotriesterase ZAPP-1
abstract: Designing a de novo phosphotriesterase requires scaffolding a dinuclear metal center bound by six catalytic residues, including a post-translationally carbamylated lysine, in a pocket that must also bind a small, flexible organophosphate and orient it for hydrolysis. We recently met this challenge using RFdiffusion3 to design the first de novo phosphotriesterases, and biochemically characterized our first hit, ZAPP-1 [1]. Here we report two crystal structures of ZAPP-1 at 1.42 and 2.28 [A] resolution. The crystal structures are nearly identical to the design model scaffold (C RMSD = 0.69, 0.71, and 0.99 [A] for three copies across two independent crystals), and the higher-resolution crystal assembles the dinuclear Zn(II) site in the designed pocket with carbamylated K16. The catalytic residues are near the designed geometry but demonstrate flexibility across the structures, albeit mostly rotameric (C{beta} RMSD [≤] 0.8 [A] for both copies in form 1). AlphaFold3 predicts the designed catalytic conformation with substrate bound and the observed crystallographic deviations without it, suggesting an induced-fit mechanism upon substrate binding. Together with prior biochemical characterization, there is strong evidence that ZAPP-1 functions as designed, validating the high precision achievable with our RFdiffusion3 design pipeline, but the structures suggest that future design should better preorganize the active site. The ability to design experimentally accurate and increasingly sophisticated enzymes directly from the computer should enable a new future of programmable catalysis and chemistry.

title: New llama-derived nanobodies enable selective detection and capture of Z-DNA
abstract: Z-DNA is a left-handed DNA conformation that forms transiently at susceptible genomic sequences during processes such as negative supercoiling and active transcription. In the cytoplasm, the innate immune receptor ZBP1 senses Z-form nucleic acids (Z-NAs, which could be DNA or RNA), triggering type I interferon production and programmed cell death. Viral infections, endogenous repetitive-element-derived RNAs, and oxidized mitochondrial DNA can generate Z-NAs, nominating them as ZBP1 agonists. Conversely, ADAR1 is proposed to recognize and edit endogenous Z-RNAs, thereby muting inappropriate innate immune responses. Both proteins engage Z-NAs through Z domains, which are evolutionarily conserved across vertebrates. Progress in defining Z-NA biology has been limited by near-exclusive reliance on the Z22 monoclonal antibody, the field's principal detection reagent. To expand the availability of distinct, validated anti-Z-NA affinity reagents, we generated and characterized llama-derived nanobodies. Llamas were immunized with brominated poly(dG:dC) DNA, and four recombinant nanobodies (nZ6, nZ6.2, nZ10, and nZ11) that bound the antigen were identified through affinity enrichment and mass spectrometry-guided discovery. The nanobodies selectively recognized Z-DNA in biochemical assays and displayed nanomolar affinities, while homodimerized nZ6.2 achieved picomolar binding. Unlike Z domains, nZ6.2 does not induce B-to-Z transitions, indicating recognition of pre-existing Z-DNA and immobilized nZ6.2 selectively co-immunoprecipitated ADAR1 and ZBP1 with Z-DNA but not B-DNA. Furthermore, nZ6.2 detected Z-DNA-related structures in a human keratinocyte cell line and in neutrophils from patients with systemic lupus erythematous, producing staining patterns overlapping those of Z22. These renewable, engineerable binders provide orthogonal reagents for investigating Z-NA biology, interferon signaling, and autoimmune disease.

title: Image-based classification of abamectin and fipronil exposure in Heteracris littoralis (Orthoptera: Acrididae) embryos using compound eye histology
abstract: Pesticide exposure is usually assessed by chemical analysis of residues, which says little about biological effect. We asked whether the compound eye of grasshopper embryos carries image features that reflect exposure. Embryos of Heteracris littoralis were treated with sublethal concentrations (LC30) of abamectin or fipronil, and ten malformed embryos per treatment and ten untreated controls were sectioned, stained with hematoxylin and eosin and photographed. The compound eye was extracted by graph-cut segmentation, thresholded, sharpened and rotated to a common orientation.

title: 8-Oxoguanine Is the Major Product of the Reaction of Guanine Radical Cations with •NO2: A Spin-Orchestrated, Anisotropic Reaction Landscape and Its Biological Implications
abstract: Formation of guanine radical cations (G•+) represents a hallmark DNA lesion produced by ionizing radiation and one-electron oxidation processes. •NO2, a reactive nitrogen species in living systems, drives nitrative and oxidative damage linked to mutagenesis and inflammation. Herein, we delineate spin-orchestrated interactions between •NO2 and radical cations of 2′-deoxyguanosine (dGuo•+) and its model compound 9-methylguanine (9MG•+) to probe synergistic pathways that exacerbate guanine nucleobase and nucleoside damage. Kinetic energy-resolved reaction coupled with mass spectrometric measurements revealed distinct pathways governing regioselective nitrite- and nitro-additions, adduct decomposition, and charge transfer. Direct dynamics simulations and potential energy surface analyses of the 9MG•+ + •NO2 model system, using spin-projected and time-dependent DFT, CCSD(T), and CASPT2 theories, characterized reaction mechanisms, thermodynamics, and kinetics arising from anisotropic interactions within open-shell 1,OS[G•+(↑)···(↓)•NO2] and 3[G•+(↑)···(↑)•NO2]. Through radical combination, the reaction system advances through multiple excited electronic and vibrational manifolds while preserving spin states (no intersystem crossing); only singlet states are open to chemical transformations. •NO2 markedly amplifies the lesion of guanine radicals by promoting sequential electron and H loss, producing 8-oxoguanine in neutral, radical cation, and doubly oxidized forms, along with release of •NO, NO+, and HNO. These pathways proceed through nitrite addition rather than guanine nitration, and HNO forms through •NO-mediated hydrogen abstraction via both conventional and roaming mechanisms. The studies identified new routes to the 8-oxoguanine lesion that has been traditionally attributed to reactive oxygen species. The biological implications of •NO2-mediated damage to guanine radical cations are discussed.

title: SAM-Dependent Precursor Peptide Engagement by Darobactin Maturase DarE
abstract: Radical S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) enzymes that synthesize structurally constrained ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) with therapeutic potential mostly do so by employing a dedicated RiPP recognition element (RRE). With the growing number of RRE-free maturases discovered, how these enzymes engage their substrates remains largely unexplored. In this work, we mapped substrate-enzyme interactions in DarE, an RRE-free radical SAM enzyme that installs the C-C and C-O-C crosslinks of the antibiotic darobactin during the first step of darobactin biosynthesis.

title: X-rays reveal fleeting intermediate step as iron-containing molecule responds to light
abstract: A research team has traced how a molecule rearranges its electrons when excited by light. The findings, published in Angewandte Chemie International Edition, help clarify a long-standing question and open new possibilities for studying chemistry in motion, such as bonds breaking or forming—fundamental steps in reactions involving catalysts and biological molecules. The collaboration included Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin (HZB), the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Villigen, Switzerland, and European XFEL.

title: Electron dynamics in graphene irradiated by a quantum wave packet versus a classical point charge
abstract: Electron irradiation is essential for materials characterization and modification, though the fundamental interactions between incident electrons and host materials remain under investigation. Using quantum-mechanical first-principles simulations, we study electron dynamics under external irradiation. While we set out to quantify differences in key observables, including kinetic energy loss, secondary electron emission, and backscattered electrons between classical and quantum-mechanical descriptions of the incident electron, we uncover an unexpected regime in which their backscattering predictions differ markedly: At an incident energy of around 400 eV, the quantum wave packet yields a finite backscattering yield, while the sampled classical ensemble predicts a vanishing yield. This wave-packet backscattering yield remains finite and gradually decreases at higher incident energies. Our results provide clear guidance for selecting appropriate computational descriptions of incident electrons based on their kinetic energy. More importantly, our results identify a targeted experimental energy window in which the classical and quantum–mechanical descriptions of the incident electron can be sensitively benchmarked. This enables the rational design and characterization of 2D materials with quantum electronic effects via high-resolution electron-beam nanofabrication techniques.

title: New mixing benchmark could help industry reduce energy use in stirred tanks
abstract: Solid–liquid mixing, where particles are dispersed in a liquid, is essential in many industrial processes such as slurry preparation, crystallization, precipitation, adsorption and dissolution. In such cases, effective mixing is critical for contact between particles and liquid, enabling mass transfer. Floating particles often pose a challenge in mixing because they are lighter than the liquid and tend to float at its surface. While impeller agitation does draw them into the liquid, the minimum mixing intensity needed for effective drawdown has been difficult to define.

title: Generative molecular design needs oracle grounding
abstract: Generative molecular design is guided by oracles, computational proxies of experimental goals that models can exploit. We argue that oracle grounding, in which experiments diagnose and correct oracle failures, will allow generative models to discover not only new molecules but also new chemistry.

title: Integrative 3D imaging and deep learning approach reveals cardiac fibroblast dynamics after myocardial infarction.
abstract: Cardiac fibroblasts (CFs) are key mediators of heart failure progression, driving fibrotic scar formation after myocardial infarction (MI). Conventional preclinical assessment of MI relies on two-dimensional histology, which cannot resolve the three-dimensional (3D) architecture of the injured heart. Understanding the molecular mechanisms of CF activation is critical for identifying new drug targets, yet spatial mapping of gene expression in intact hearts remains challenging.

title: Molecular Dynamics Simulation of the Solidification of AlCoCuFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Nanowire
abstract: Molecular dynamics simulation of the solidification behavior of an AlCoCuFeNi high-entropy alloy nanowire was performed using an embedded atom model potential at cooling rates of 10^11, 10^12, and 10^13 K/s. Periodic boundary conditions were applied along the nanowire axis to model an effectively infinite nanowire. The crystallization process was characterized through the temperature dependence of the potential energy. Structural evolution was analyzed using adaptive common-neighbor analysis (CNA) and radial distribution functions (RDF). The results show that the final structure changes from amorphous to crystalline with decreasing cooling rate, demonstrating the strong influence of cooling conditions on phase formation in nanoscale high-entropy alloy systems.

title: Chips smaller than rice grains wirelessly track heat during chemical reactions
abstract: A fleck-sized chip at the bottom of a test tube can provide researchers with data for every second of a chemical reaction while it is occurring.

title: Biocatalytic Carboligation As a Versatile Route to (Rare) monosaccharides
abstract: Rare monosaccharides have emerged as valuable building blocks for the chemical manufacturing of pharmaceuticals and food additives. Although numerous biocatalytic strategies have focused on the interconversion of naturally abundant sugars, bottom-up enzymatic synthesis from smaller carbon sources represents an increasingly attractive alternative route that offers high stereochemical control. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the de novo (or bottom-up) enzymatic synthesis of monosaccharides through carbon–carbon bond-forming biocatalysis (i.e., carboligation).

title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
abstract: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.

title: High-throughput electrochemical transformation expands mass spectrometric reference space for transformation products
abstract: Structure annotation of unknown features detected by high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry remains challenging. Spectral libraries provide confident annotation but have limited chemical space coverage. This hampers discovery of natural products and xenobiotics and often necessitates laborious isolation and characterization. We introduce a scalable high-throughput workflow combining online electrochemistry with high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry to expand the empirical spectral reference space for transformation products. This approach enables generating thousands of potential transformation products used for prioritization in non-target datasets. Applying the workflow to 112 chemicals, we generated a suspect spectral library containing 1,341 transformation product entries. Repository-scale matching against public non-target datasets yielded matches for 214 electrochemical transformation products with 70% not annotated by conventional open-access spectral libraries. This workflow provides a source of empirical reference spectra for overlooked transformation products, extends coverage beyond compounds represented in conventional libraries, and supports prioritization of features for structural elucidation, quantification, and bioactivity assessment.

title: Recent progress and challenges in Schiff base-based optical chemosensors
abstract: The traditional analytical methods for detecting environmentally or biologically important analytes are sensitive, but not suitable for rapid on-site analysis because they require complex instrumentation and laboratory facilities. Optical Schiff base-based chemosensors and biosensors are promising tools owing to their tunable photophysical properties, and colorimetry or fluorescence sensing modes.

title: Deep learning-based conversion of MRI to synthetic CT for gamma knife radiosurgery – A large-sample study
abstract: Purpose Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS) relies on planning computed tomography (CT) for dose calculation, which introduces inherent CT/MR registration errors, unnecessary radiation exposure, and suboptimal soft-tissue contrast. While deep learning-based synthetic CT (sCT) generation from MRI offers a promising solution, existing studies predominantly utilize small sample sizes (typically fewer than 100 cases), which may limit prediction accuracy.

title: Applications of computer vision in mosquito-borne diseases: A systematic review.
abstract: Mosquito-borne diseases (MBDs) remain a major global health challenge. Vector surveillance, pathogen detection, and clinical diagnosis are central to control efforts but are limited by labor-intensive workflows and shortages of trained personnel. Computer vision (CV) offers opportunities for scalable automation throughout the MBD management pipeline. We aimed to systematically characterize the applications of computer vision in mosquito-borne diseases research, summarize methodological developments, and identify opportunities and barriers to translating these advances into public health…

title: Temporal blood sampling improves parameter recovery in a model of enterohepatic bile acid circulation using surrogate-accelerated Bayesian inference
abstract: Bile acids (BAs) are essential signaling molecules whose enterohepatic circulation (EHC) is disrupted across hepatobiliary disorders. Despite their potential as biomarkers, clinical utility is limited by high inter-individual variability, the inability of accessible peripheral blood to reflect true hepatic exposure, and the difficulty of directly measuring key physiological parameters governing the EHC.

title: Randomized Subsystem Descent for Fermion-to-Qubit Mapping
abstract: We propose a versatile and efficient algorithmic framework for optimizing Fermion-to-qubit mappings by generalizing the idea of randomized block coordinate descent. Our greedy approach, termed Randomized Subsystem Descent, iteratively samples a tractable subsystem from the full Hamiltonian, performs optimization within the subsystem under a given metric, and then reintegrates the updated subsystem into the global operator.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Neglected Tropical Diseases: Current Applications, Challenges, and Opportunities
abstract: Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) affect more than one billion people globally, disproportionately burdening populations in low-resource tropical and subtropical settings. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer considerable opportunities to strengthen NTD control, yet the scope, maturity, and translational readiness of AI applications across this disease portfolio remain incompletely characterized.

title: The retention of nanoparticles in solid tumours
abstract: Interactions between nanoparticles and tumour components after entering and before exiting govern retention of the nanoparticles. A computational framework is reported to predict nanoparticle residence time and, hence, to guide treatment.

title: Chemoselective Denitrification of Nitrate to Molecular Nitrogen Catalyzed by Guest Transition Metals in Host Keplerate Nanocapsules
abstract: The combination of supramolecular chemistry and catalysis is a powerful tool to engender reactions in confined space. Broadly, this combination can also be viewed as a method to functionally mimic redox metalloenzymes. Herein, we have prepared guest–host nanocapsules based on a porous, {MoV60WVI72}, inorganic Keplerate host internally lined with circa 20 imidazole acetate (ImA) ligands as histidine surrogates, {MoV60WVI72-ImA}. This enabled the encapsulation of approximately 10 Cu(II) or Fe(III) guest active sites, yielding M10⊂{W72Mo60-ImA} (M = CuII, FeIII). These compounds were characterized by various NMR techniques and XPS. Interest in electrocatalytic nitrate reduction has been flourishing in recent years, with NH3 as typically the only product under protic conditions via a dissimilatory reduction pathway. The formation of N2 via a denitrification pathway requires N–N bond formation that can be amplified by reactions in confined space. The investigation of electrocatalytic nitrate reduction catalyzed by M10⊂{W72Mo60-ImA} revealed up to a ∼10:1 preference via N–N bond formation, leading to N2O and N2 within the nanocapsule. Cu10⊂{W72Mo60-Im} was more active and at lower potentials compared to Fe10⊂{W72Mo60-ImA}. 15N guest exchange saturation transfer NMR measurements indicate a low population of NO3– within the capsule albeit in fast exchange with the surrounding aqueous solution. Despite this, quantitative yields were observed under optimal conditions. Dissection of the denitrification pathway indicates the formation of N2O and N2 as major observable products. Intermediate NO2– and NO are transient and quickly reduced since their accumulation leads to nanocapsule decomposition. The Keplerate-based guest–host nanocapsules determined chemoselectivity by control of the reaction pathway.

title: Terahertz Stimulation Enhances Nanopore Capture Rate via Mitigating Voltage-Induced Water Compression
abstract: Nanopore sensing has emerged as a powerful tool for proteomic analysis, yet controlling molecular translocation, particularly for neutral residues, remains a significant challenge. Here, we use all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the translocation of electrically neutral peptides and amino acids, and to elucidate how nanoslit geometry and applied voltage jointly regulate the process from both kinetic and thermodynamic perspectives. As the applied voltage increases from 0 to 1 V, the biomolecule capture time doubles, whereas the dwell time is reduced by half.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Multi-Omic Profiling for Molecular Diagnosis of Erythrodermic Skin Diseases.
abstract: Erythroderma is one of the most challenging clinical scenarios in modern dermatology. It represents an acute, potentially life-threatening inflammatory condition characterised by erythema and scaling affecting more than 90% of the skin surface, with mortality rates up to 9%. Various underlying skin diseases cause erythroderma yet are difficult to distinguish clinically and histopathologically. This poses a major diagnostic challenge and delays targeted therapy, with potentially severe acute and long-term consequences.
